body.heading: Luck first, knowledge later
paragraphs: In the matching-pairs game - cards face down, flip two, keep them if they match - the early game is mostly chance. Suppose 24 cards lie face down. You flip one; its partner is exactly one of the 23 remaining cards, so a blind second flip matches with probability 1 in 23, about 4 percent. Early matches are gifts, not skill.

But every card you have ever seen and remembered changes the game. A card flipped and lost is not wasted - it is information banked. Once you know where both copies of a pair are sitting, a match becomes certain rather than lucky. The whole arc of the game is the conversion of luck into knowledge.

body.heading: How the good players actually play
paragraphs: Strong players obey one rule early: always flip an unknown card first. Flipping a card you already know first teaches you nothing new; flipping an unknown one might complete a pair you half-know, and at worst adds a new location to your map. Only when your first flip matches something in memory do you spend a known card as the second flip.

Memory itself can be engineered. Narrate locations silently ('the frog is top-left'), group the board into neighbourhoods, and attach pairs to little stories. Most people can hold only a handful of unrelated locations at once, but chunking - remembering 'the top row is frog, star, moon' as one item instead of three - stretches that handful considerably.

body.heading: Try it yourself
paragraphs: Play a round with 6 pairs, then a round with 12, and count how many locations you can reliably hold. Note the moment in the 12-pair game where the board flips from foggy to familiar - that is the information tipping point, and it arrives earlier as your chunking improves.

For a probability postscript, compute the blind-match chance at the start of the 6-pair game: after your first flip, the partner is 1 of 11 remaining cards. Compare that friendly 1-in-11 with the 1-in-23 of the bigger game, and you can feel why small decks feel lucky and big decks feel earned.

takeaway: Early flips buy information and late flips spend it - the player who treats every revealed card as treasure wins the endgame.
